title: The end of al-Hashr
tomorrow: why does a bedtime surah tell you to look at the sky again?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Hadid: the First and the Last, and with you wherever you are. Today, more of His names, poured out one after another.

Every contact in your phone gets one name, maybe an emoji. Nobody you love fits in it. The end of al-Hashr starts with something even bigger failing to hold up. In Pickthall's words: "If We had caused this Qur'an to descend upon a mountain, thou (O Muhammad) verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah." A mountain, cracking. And right after it, a flood of names.
screen: `ONE NAME PER CONTACT.` → `A MOUNTAIN, HUMBLED.` → `A FLOOD OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: The question underneath is old: can any name hold God? The passage opens by turning to the listener: "let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow." Then a line worth telling a friend: don't be like those who forgot God, so that He made them forget themselves. Forget God, the verse says, and you lose track of your own soul. Then the mountain. Then the names, in a rush: "He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord, the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Majestic, the Compeller, the Superb." And: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. His are the most beautiful names." The answer here: no single name holds Him, so the names come many, each one a window, and every one of them begins with He is Allah. Now a neighbor. In the Torah, God passes before Moses and proclaims who He is, in the JPS words: "merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." Jewish tradition treasures those attributes of mercy and recites them on solemn days. The shared ground: both reach for God through names of mercy. And an honest difference. Muslims call on God by the beautiful names aloud, in prayer and dhikr. In Jewish practice, the holiest name, written with four letters, isn't spoken; readers say Adonai, my Lord, in its place. One way honors God by calling on many names. The other honors a name by keeping it unspoken.
screen: `FORGET GOD, FORGET YOURSELF.` · `NAMES IN A RUSH.` · `THE TORAH: MERCIFUL AND GRACIOUS.` · `CALLED ALOUD, OR KEPT UNSPOKEN.` · then, large: `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL NAMES.`

segments.voice: Read the list slowly, pausing at each name: the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Creator, the Fashioner. Then take a pen and write by hand the one that stopped you. Hold that single name through the sit.
screen: `PAUSE AT EACH NAME.` · `WRITE THE ONE THAT STOPPED YOU.`

segments.voice: The end of al-Hashr: the last verses of surah 59, a humbled mountain and a cascade of the most beautiful names.
Carry this: the most beautiful names, many windows onto one God. The list is yours now.

'Jewish tradition treasures those attributes of mercy and recites them on solemn days' refers to the Thirteen Attributes (Shelosh Esreh Middot) said on fast days and the High Holy Days; no count is stated. 'Every one of them begins with He is Allah' describes 59:22–24, where each run of names follows 'He is Allah'. Confirm.
